analysis.one_liner: Requires websites to remove a person's name-and-address or phone information on request.
analysis.headline: The Cyber Privacy Act, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any public website that lists a person's name together with their address or phone number to post a clear way for that person to request removal, and to promptly take the information down when asked. The Federal Trade Commission would have enforced it the same way it enforces rules against unfair or deceptive business practices. The bill never got past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose names, addresses, or phone numbers appear on public websites would gain a legal right to have that information taken down. This most directly affects people harassed online, stalking victims, and anyone who finds their home address listed on a people-search or directory site without an easy way to remove it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People whose addresses or phone numbers are posted online

how_it_helps.text: Any website that publicly displays a person's name along with their address or phone number would have to provide a clearly located way to request removal of that information.
Once a person requests removal, the website would have to promptly take the personal information down.

Violations would be treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the Federal Trade Commission Act, giving the FTC authority to enforce the removal requirement with its existing powers and penalties.

analysis.who_pays: Websites that publish personal information — including people-search sites, online directories, and social platforms — would bear the cost of building removal request systems, reviewing requests, and taking down listings, and would lose the page views and ad revenue that come from searchable personal data.

drawbacks.text: The requirement covers 'any Internet website' that displays name plus address or phone number, with no carve-outs for news organizations, public records reposts, or small sites, so compliance could be burdensome and raise tension with publishing and First Amendment interests.
'Promptly remove' is undefined and the bill places the burden on individuals to find their own listings and request removal, so the protection depends on people knowing where their data appears.
The bill gives no private right of action described in its text; enforcement rests entirely on FTC action, which historically moves case by case and leaves many violations unaddressed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a real, if narrow, protection: a right to opt out of having your name-plus-address or phone number displayed publicly. It was drafted broadly and vaguely — covering virtually every website, with no exceptions and no definition of 'promptly' — so it would likely have needed refinement to avoid sweeping in news sites, government records reposts, and small publishers. As a one-page bill with zero cosponsors, it was more a statement of principle than a finished law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor action until the two-year Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Thaddeus McCotter introduced the Cyber Privacy Act in the House on April 22, 2010.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which was its only committee referral.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — was ever recorded on the bill before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Websites and data brokers that profit from publishing names, addresses, and phone numbers are better off, because the removal requirement never took effect. People whose personal information appears on such sites gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Thaddeus McCotter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cyber Privacy Act on April 22, 2010.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Chair Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration during the remainder of the 111th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsor introduced the bill and no other member of either party signed on, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition can be read from the record.

industries.industry: People-search sites and online data brokers
industries.note: These sites make money by publishing names, addresses, and phone numbers — exactly the data the bill would have required them to remove on request. Their business model depends on the data staying up, which is the opposite of what people whose information is listed want.

industries.industry: Websites and social media platforms generally
industries.note: Any site displaying personal information would have had to build a removal-request system and take down listings promptly, a real compliance cost, while losing the traffic and ad revenue that searchable personal data generates.
